                 Abstract
                 Carbon, Capture, and Storage (CCS) plays a pivotal role in unlocking production from sour gas fields. For
                 a recent PTTEP greenfield development in Sarawak, Malaysia, hydrocarbon gas containing carbon dioxide
                 (CO2) above 15 mol% must be treated to meet sale specifications. To develop the hydrocarbon resources with
                 the least Greenhouse Gas (GHG) intensity, CO2 captured from gas production will need to be transported
                 and injected offshore into depleted reservoirs.
                    The behavior of CO2 up to the storage reservoirs must be extensively investigated to overcome challenges
                 on corrosion, injectivity, and low temperature. A PVT analysis was originally done in the front-end design
                 stage to define the phase envelope of the injected CO2 in relation to the contaminants from the gas treatment
                 system. Subsequently, steady state and dynamic flow assurance assessments of the integrated CO2 transport
                 and injection network were conducted to determine the safe operating window for the overall system. Key
                 findings were then translated into functional design requirements for the CCS facilities such as the transport
                 pipeline and injection platform.
                    To mitigate hydrate risks at the well bottom-hole and keep CO2 along the transport pipeline and injection
                 wellhead platform in supercritical phase, CO2 injection must closely adhere to the established pressure,
                 temperature, and flow rate envelopes based on the flow assurance analysis. Once all storage reservoirs
                 are sufficiently pressurized, the arrival temperature of CO2 at the injection platform no longer needs to be
                 controlled which will allow CO2 to be injected at seabed temperature with no adverse risks in the wellbore.
                    Several facility design options to achieve the desired CO2 injection pressure and temperature at the remote
                 wellhead platform were then assessed resulting in the most cost-effective and energy-efficient decision to
                 insulate the subsea transport pipeline. Dynamic flow assurance study results were also included to operating
                 philosophies enabling the CO2 transport system to be started up and restarted even under the most onerous
                 pipeline shut-in scenarios and environmental circumstances. For possible issues with trace impurities in the
                 captured CO2, such as TEG, the fluid specifications at the inlet of the transport pipeline are tightly controlled
                 and considered satisfactory in minimizing the severe corrosion risk in the downstream facilities.
                    In developing this greenfield initiative with minimal GHG emission, understanding the flow behaviors
                 along the transport and injection network is crucial to enable up to 2.0 MTPA of CO2 injection into depleted

                 Introduction
                 As the demand for Carbon, Capture, and Storage (CCS) continues to grow to abate global carbon dioxide
                 (CO2) emissions, more depleted hydrocarbon reservoirs are being converted into CO2 storage reservoirs.
                 Unlike saline aquifers, depleted reservoirs can be rapidly characterized and converted to CO2 storages due
                 to the vast amount of geological data accumulated over the production phase. Despite their developmental
                 benefits, depleted reservoirs are often low in pressure at the start of CO2 injection. For a recent PTTEP
                 greenfield development in Sarawak, Malaysia, hydrocarbon gas containing carbon dioxide (CO2) above 15
                 mol% must be treated to meet sale specifications. In order to develop the hydrocarbon resources with the
                 least Greenhouse Gas (GHG) intensity, CO2 must be captured and transported 40 km offshore for injection
                 into depleted hydrocarbon reservoirs. Through a flow assurance modelling perspective, this paper aims
                 to identify the thermohydraulic challenges associated with CO2 injection in depleted storage sites and to
                 provide a conceptual design framework for establishing a safe operating window to overcome challenges
                 with low temperature, injectivity, and corrosion in low-pressure reservoirs during steady state and transient
                 scenarios.

                 Project Overview
                 The CO2 that will be sequestered as part of this greenfield initiative will be captured by a solvent-based
                 gas treatment unit at an onshore processing plant. Once captured, CO2 is then compressed and dehydrated
                 before flowing into the transport pipeline. Although CO2 is transported to the injection platform in dense /
                 supercritical phase, a stringent water content is still required to prevent free water drop out and hydrate
                 formation along the pipeline and offshore facility during low temperature scenarios (e.g., pressure letdowns,
                 depressurization, etc.).

                     The CO2 storage site for this development is located 40 km offshore from the gas processing plant and
                 consists of multiple sandstone hydrocarbon reservoirs that will be depleted at the start of CO2 injection.
                 Although the reservoirs have been producing for more than fifteen (15) years, the integrities of the caprock
                 and fault at this site are still effective. At depletion, the reservoirs provide sufficient storage capacities
                 for sequestrating CO2 from the gas processing plant throughout its design life. All existing hydrocarbon
                 production wells at the offshore CO2 storage site will be plugged and abandoned prior to starting CO2
                 injection to minimize potential leak paths. New injection wells designed specifically for CO2 service will
                 be drilled and completed for each reservoir.
                     For this specific CO2 storage site, multiple depleted reservoirs will be utilized. The reservoirs vary in
                 depth, pressure, and permeability, but they can be categorized into three (3) groups: i) shallow reservoirs,
                 ii) intermediate reservoirs, and iii) deep reservoirs. The representative features of each category of CO2

                 CO2 compressors to each reservoir contact. Critical to the analysis, the CO2 injection choke valves were

                 the injected CO2 stream. As a conservative approach, the CO2 fluid temperature at the well bottom-hole is
                 also limited above 10°C to minimize hydrate risk near the reservoir contact.

                 CO2 Thermohydraulic Behavior in Depleted Reservoirs
                 From the design constraints in the previous section, a steady state analysis was first conducted to investigate
                 the option of injecting CO2 at seabed temperature into the storage reservoirs. With the pressure upstream
                 of the choke valve on the injection platform set at 80 barg, the early-life tubing pressure and temperature
                 profiles for CO2 injection at various flow rates between the turndown and design capacities of each well
                 into the intermediate reservoir (Pres ~30 barg) and deep reservoir (Pres ~50 barg) are shown in Figure 4.

                 remain above the minimum design temperature of the piping downstream of the choke valves (-46°C) if
                 it were injected at seabed temperature into the intermediate and deep reservoirs. However, low CO2 fluid
                 temperatures are expected at both the SCSSV (< -7°C) and well bottom-hole (< 10°C) for the intermediate

                 reservoir. The CO2 fluid temperature at the SCSSV is dictated by the J-T effect across the choke valve
                 as the pressure is reduced from 80 barg to the early-life Injection Tubing Head Pressure (ITHP) at the
                 wellhead. At the turndown injection capacity, minor contributions from the friction loss in the injection
                 tubing and pressure drop across the perforation at the reservoir contact will lead to a relatively low ITHP
                 and subsequently a CO2 fluid temperature at the SCSSV as low as -12.7°C. At higher flow rates up to
                 the well's design capacity, a higher friction loss in the tubing will lead to a higher ITHP at the wellhead
                 which will reduce the J-T effect across the choke valve resulting in temperatures above -7°C at the SCSSV.
                 Evident from the behavior of CO2 in depleted reservoirs, the CO2 fluid temperature above the SCSSV can
                 be controlled above the minimum design temperature constraint by one of the following:

                           • Reducing the J-T cooling effect across the injection choke valve; or
                           • Increasing the turndown flow rate of each well during early-life operation; or
                           • Setting the SCSSV deeper in the injection tubing to allow the CO2 fluid temperature to increase
                                prior to contacting the valve.
                    Regardless of the temperature at the SCSSV, the temperature at the well bottom-hole for the intermediate
                 reservoir will always be below 10°C. Even though the CO2 fluid temperature at the turndown flow rate is
                 observed to rise along the injection tubing, the J-T cooling effect at the wellhead cannot be offset by the
                 temperature increment due to the compression effect from gravity and heat transfer into the wellbore from
                 the surrounding rock formation. On the contrary, the CO2 fluid temperature will continue to drop as the gas
                 is continuously expanded along the wellbore for CO2 injection at higher flow rates. Under this scenario,
                 heat transfer from the surrounding is also less effective resulting in a well bottom-hole temperature lower
                 than 10°C.
                    Conversely, CO2 fluid temperatures lower than the design limits at both the SCSSV and well bottom-
                 hole are not observed in the deep reservoir. As the CO2 density increases with the reservoir pressure, the
                 pressure of the CO2 stream will continue to rise throughout the trajectory as the compression effect from
                 gravity outweighs the resistance from the friction loss in the injection tubing. In this situation, the CO2 fluid
                 temperature will continue to increase as it flows through the wellbore.
                    In summary, CO2 injection at seabed temperature is not feasible for all reservoir conditions except the
                 deep reservoir in this development. As a result, the temperature of the CO2 fluid stream arriving at the
                 injection platform must be increased to compensate the J-T effect across the choke valve and subsequent
                 cooling in the wellbore from friction loss in the injection tubing.

                 Early-Life Operation
                 To define the early-life operating conditions, a sensitivity analysis investigating the effects of the CO2
                 injection temperature (upstream of choke valve) on the well bottom-hole temperature was conducted, and
                 the results are shown in Figure 5. For this study, the pressure upstream of the choke valve was controlled at
                 80 barg while the properties of the intermediate reservoir (start of injection reservoir pressure) were used
                 as the boundary conditions due to it being the main injection target with the largest storage volume. Figure
                 5 shows that 50°C is the most optimal CO2 injection temperature upstream of the choke valve with respect
                 to the intermediate reservoir. At this injection temperature, the well bottom-hole temperature is expected to
                 be 17°C. Increasing the CO2 injection temperature to 60°C can increase the difference between the bottom-
                 hole temperature and the design constraint, but it will also decrease the maximum flow rate achievable in
                 each injection well (~20% reduction) – due to the increased CO2 volumetric flow rate and friction loss in
                 the injection tubing – which is undesirable.

                    For reservoirs shallower than the intermediate reservoir, a CO2 injection temperature of 50°C is
                 insufficient as the well is not deep enough for heat transfer from the surrounding rock formation to
                 compensate the temperature drop in the wellbore from fluid expansion. Instead of increasing the injection
                 temperature, an alternative is to limit the maximum injection flow into the shallower reservoirs allowing
                 CO2 to be warmed up by the surrounding formation. From Figure 6, CO2 injection into the shallow reservoir
                 during early-life operation must not exceed 37.5% of the well's design capacity to keep the bottom-
                 hole temperature above 10°C. At these conditions, the maximum flow rate for the deep reservoir is also
                 hydraulically restricted at 80% of the well's design capacity by the available injection pressure of 80 barg.
                 Further raising the injection pressure beyond 80 barg will considerably impact the bottom-hole temperatures
                 in the other reservoirs.

                 Late-Life Operation
                 As the CO2 fluid temperature at the well bottom-hole is a strong function of the reservoir pressure,
                 another sensitivity analysis was performed to identify the minimum pressure of the depleted reservoir
                 that will enable CO2 to be injected at seabed temperature without the requirement for elevated operating
                 temperatures. From Figure 7, all reservoirs at the CO2 storage site must be pressurized above 50 barg to
                 ensure that the CO2 fluid temperature at the bottom-hole of each injection well remains above 10°C.




                                                       Figure 7—Effects of Reservoir Pressure on the Well Bottom-Hole Temperature


                    During late-life operation, CO2 can be injected at seabed temperature as its behavior in the injection well
                 is dominated by gravity / compression effects. The injection pressure, however, will have to be adjusted
                 from 80 to 100 barg to account for the higher reservoir pressures.

                 Design of CO2 Transport and Injection Network
                 Several design options were assessed to raise the CO2 fluid temperature to 50°C upon arrival at the offshore
                 injection platform. Additionally, the possibility to avoid low CO2 fluid temperatures at the bottom-hole of
                 each injection well by transporting and injecting CO2 in gas phase was also studied. The three (3) options
                 considered are described as follows:

                           • Option 1: Pipeline Insulation
                                   The CO2 transport pipeline will be coated with dry insulation to preserve the CO2 fluid
                                temperature from the compression train at the gas processing plant. During the early-life reservoir
                                pressurization phase, the discharge aftercooler of the final-stage CO2 compressor will be partially
                                bypassed enabling CO2 to enter the transport pipeline at a maximum temperature of 110°C.
                                Accounting for the system's turndown capacity, the thickness of the dry insulation is specified at

                           • Option 2: Offshore Electric Heater

                             outlet to 50°C upstream of the choke valves. Under this scenario, CO2 will be transported in dense /

                             renewable power generation at the injection platform is not feasible. Instead, subsea power cables

                           • Option 3: Gas-Phase CO2 Injection
                                Gaseous CO2 will be transported and injected into the depleted reservoir to reduce the J-T effect

                             the injection platform will be restricted at 50 barg for gas-phase operation. With the lower density of

                    Based on the techno-economic comparison in the table above, the option to insulate the CO2 transport
                 pipeline was selected as it requires the least capital upfront. When compared to installing an offshore electric
                 heater, insulating the CO2 transport pipeline is also more energy efficient as the heat of compression from the

                 cannot be sustained with gas-phase CO2 injection without increasing the well count and/or the injection
                 tubing size given that the upstream choke pressure is limited at 50 barg.

                 Transient Operations
                 Although the low temperature concerns in the depleted reservoirs can be managed during steady state
                 injection, transient operations such as initial start-up and restarts present a different challenge as the CO2
                 stream will not be at the required injection temperature (i.e., 50°C) during these scenarios. Dynamic flow
                 assurance analysis was then conducted using the integrated pipeline-well OLGA model to develop the
                 operating philosophies allowing the CO2 transport and injection network to be started up and restarted safely
                 within the system's design boundaries.

                 Initial Start-Up
                 During initial start-up, the CO2 injection wells will be completed with a liquid column. CO2 injection is
                 scheduled to commence after the CO2 transport pipeline is pressurized to its normal operating pressure (i.e.,
                 80 barg). Significant J-T cooling across the injection choke valve is expected as the equilibrium pressure and
                 temperature above the liquid column (downstream of the choke valve) is close to atmospheric conditions
                 (i.e., 0 barg and ambient temperature). Without backpressure at the wellhead, the CO2 fluid temperature
                 downstream of the choke valve can reach -64.6°C for a short period of time. In order to avoid inner wall metal
                 temperatures falling below the design constraints, a relative fast well ramp-up rate need to be considered.
                 Regardless of the ramp-up rate, CO2 injection into the shallow and intermediate reservoirs can result in well
                 bottom-hole temperatures below 10°C. In these cases, a hydrate inhibitor will be injected until the bottom-
                 hole temperature exceeds 10°C.

                 Restarts
                 Low temperature concerns in the wellbore also need to be circumvented when the CO2 transport and
                 injection network is restarted during early-life operation. If the system is shut down for a short period of
                 time before the fluid temperature in the CO2 transport pipeline falls below 50°C, the CO2 injection wells can
                 be restarted immediately. From the pipeline shut-in temperature profiles in Figure 8, the "no touch time"
                 of the system is about two (2) hours.




                                                Figure 8—Temperature Profiles in the CO2 Transport Pipeline During Shut-In Conditions


                    For prolonged shutdowns, the fluid temperature in the CO2 transport pipeline will drop to the seabed
                 temperature. To restart CO2 injection in this scenario, it is necessary to start-up the system by first injecting
                 CO2 into the deep reservoir to bring the injection temperature back to 50°C (Figure 9). After stabilizing the
                 pipeline outlet temperature, CO2 injection into the other shallower reservoirs can then resume without any
                 low temperature concerns even if the shut-in tubing head pressure is as low as 25 barg (Figure 10).

                 Conclusions and Recommendations
                 For this greenfield initiative, CO2 injection in depleted hydrocarbon reservoirs proves to be not only viable
                 but also sustainable in reducing GHG emission. However, low temperatures in the CO2 injection wells
                 – in particular at the Surface Control Subsurface Safety Valve (SCSSV) and bottom-hole are expected
                 when the reservoir pressures of the CO2 storages are relatively low. Understanding the CO2 fluid behaviors
                 and tendencies in the transport and injection network through fluid characterization exercises and steady
                 state / dynamic flow assurance analysis is vital in defining the required pressure, temperature, and flow rate
                 envelopes and optimizing facility design requirements to safely inject CO2 into depleted reservoirs.
